title: Making Weak Interlayer Excitons Absorb: Manipulating the Effective Oscillator Strength via Purcell Engineering of Critical Coupling
authors: Saroj Poudyal, Anabel Atash Kahlon, Michael Klein, Matan Meshulam, Yonatan Gershuni, Thomas Poirier, James H. Edgar, Mukesh Kumar, Seth Ariel Tongay, Itai Epstein
abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. However, the large electron-hole separation underlying their dipolar character also results in a significantly reduced oscillator strength, limiting their direct optical interaction with light, and thus the direct probing of their dynamics and many-body interactions. Here, we show that by using Purcell engineering of critical coupling, a weak interlayer transition can absorb as strongly as the dominant intralayer transition, despite its much smaller intrinsic oscillator strength. Using this approach, in an open cavity architecture we demonstrate an order of magnitude IX absorption modulation in bilayer and trilayer MoS2, with doubling of the IX to A-exciton interaction strength weight from ~23% to ~53%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a tailored closed cavity architecture, the IX enhancement can reach beyond an order of magnitude, from ~5% to ~83% excitonic absorption, enabling IX absorption similar to intralayer excitons. An analytical description of the interaction is obtained via a closed-form transmission-line model which separates the excitonic and photonic contributions to the optical response, revealing how cavity architecture can be designed towards critical coupling. Our findings establish Purcell engineering of critical coupling as a general route to controlling and enhancing weak excitonic transitions.
summary: The research addresses the challenge of weakly interacting interlayer excitons in TMD bilayers by utilizing Purcell engineering within optical cavities. By modeling the system with a transmission-line approach, the authors show that tuning the cavity geometry can selectively enhance the IX absorption, allowing for strong optical probing comparable to the dominant intralayer transitions. This establishes critical coupling engineering as a general tool for controlling weak excitonic dynamics.
main_problem: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in TMD bilayers have weak intrinsic oscillator strengths due to large electron-hole separation, limiting their direct optical probing.
main_result: Purcell engineering of critical coupling can selectively enhance the weak IX transition, achieving absorption modulation up to an order of magnitude in open cavities and reaching 83% excitonic absorption in closed cavities.
method: The study combines theoretical modeling using a closed-form transmission-line model (TLM) with experimental measurements of reflection-contrast spectra in engineered optical cavity architectures.
model_or_system: The system involves IXs in TMD bilayers (e.g., MoS2) placed within van der Waals heterostructures that form optical cavities. The optical response is modeled using Lorentzian susceptibility and analyzed via the TLM, which accounts for cavity-modified radiative decay rates ($\gamma_r$).
key_observables: IX and A exciton absorption spectra, Purcell factor ($\zeta$), and the effective oscillator strength ($W$).
important_parameters: Critical coupling regime ($\gamma_r = \gamma_{nr}$), cavity thicknesses (hBN layers, top/bottom mirrors), and temperature (5 K to 290 K).
main_assumptions: The optical response can be accurately described by a transmission-line model separating excitonic and photonic contributions; the system is analyzed under the assumption of cavity-mediated coupling.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic band structures, device geometries, and measured reflection-contrast spectra demonstrating the weak IX resonance. Additional figures detail temperature dependence and the optimization of cavity parameters (e.g., top gold thickness) to maximize enhancement.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of weak IX absorption. It then develops the theoretical framework using the TLM to predict Purcell enhancement by tuning cavity parameters. Experimentally, it demonstrates this enhancement in open cavities, followed by a detailed analysis of closed-cavity structures to achieve near-intralayer exciton absorption levels.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it demonstrates precise, active control over weak quantum optical transitions (excitons) by engineering the photonic environment (Purcell effect) to reach critical coupling. It provides a general blueprint for enhancing weak quantum emitters.

The superstrate is dashed as it may be absent, a thin metal film, or a Bragg stack. (b) Equivalent circuit, each bulk layer a line section of admittance Yj = njε0c and propagation constant kz,j, and the bilayer a shunt admittance σ(ω) bridging the line at its own plane. Arrows give the direction of view. Yabove and Ybelow are the admittances seen looking up and down from the bilayer plane, and together with eYabove they fix the optical response of any geometry treated here (Table SIII).

The abscissa is the TLM value and the ordinate the measured peak absorption. All six operating points lie on the undercoupled branch, with the IX where the curve is steep and the A exciton where it has already flattened. FIG. 5. Experimental realization of the closed cavity. (a) Device schematic of air / Au(dg=25 nm) / hBN / bilayer MoS2 / hBN / Au. (b) Absorption of bilayer MoS2 in closed cavity. The A exciton and the IX are marked. (c) Purcell fac- tor ζ(E) for closed cavity (solid) and for the antinode open cavity device I (dashed), with the four resonance energies marked. The open cavity is nearly flat across the excitonic window and therefore presents a similar photonic environment to every resonance, whereas the closed cavity varies by nearly a factor of three and gives the IX a Purcell factor ≈2.3 times that of the A exciton.
